title: Cloze Test for Reading Comprehension (NN/g)
topic: cloze test for comprehension of plain text
rule: Blank every Nth word (typical N=6), each participant works alone, score the percent of correct guesses with synonyms and misspellings accepted. Average of 60% or more means the text is reasonably comprehensible for that audience. Test only with the real target audience: a low score can mean missing domain knowledge, not bad writing. No sample size is given.
example: 15 blanks: at least 9 correct. A low score on 'poking' in Facebook's privacy policy reflected unfamiliarity with Facebook.

title: Guest post: looking at the different ways to test content (GDS blog, with 18F)
topic: content test menu: cloze, A/B, open questions, own-words, preference, readability formulas
rule: Cloze suits technical content (finance, regulation, health). Sample as many readers as possible. Choose deletion by formula (every 5th word) or selectively; accept synonyms or only exact answers. A/B shows which version wins, not why. Pair preference tests with 'explain it in your own words' so a person judges understanding. Readability formulas miss word order and nuance. Note: the case is the US FEC site, not GOV.UK itself.
example: FEC passages of at least 150 words, every 5th word removed, synonyms accepted, target 50% accuracy, actual scores 65% to 98%. NHS organ-donation test compared 8 variants by sign-up rate.

title: Content highlighter testing (Digital.gov user research guide, from 18F)
rule: Participants mark text they find clear in one colour and confusing in another (variant: makes me feel confident vs less confident). Fix colour meanings and write instructions first; run on paper, in person or online. Discuss the marks afterwards and ask why. Compare across sessions and prioritise fixes. The guide gives no sample size and no limits. Scottish service manual calls it 'pens of power' and asks what words the user would use instead (snippet).

title: Testing Content with Users (NN/g)
topic: moderated probes for comprehension, vocabulary and tone
rule: Prefer moderated sessions with a facilitator. Ask the reader to summarise in their own words: if they can without rereading, they understood. Ask 'What does the word X mean to you?' to find jargon. Ask 'Imagine a person said these words to you. Who would that person be?' for tone. Unmoderated remote testing is discouraged for content because people rush; sessions typically 20 to 30 minutes.
llm_tell: The tone probe ('who would say this?') is a human-panel check for a generic assistant voice; the page does not say this.

title: Cloze Test for Reading Comprehension (NN/g), search-result claims on readability
rule: Readability is a property of the text alone; comprehension is text plus a specific audience. No formula measures whether users understand the site. Same page reports a cloze study of privacy policies where scores on an iPhone-sized screen were about half the desktop scores, while a later 276-participant NN/g study found no practical difference (snippet).

title: Gronier 2016, validity of the 5-second test (Journal of Usability Studies), with Kuric et al. 2024 (Behaviour & Information Technology)
rule: The five-second test captures first impressions, mostly hedonic and look-and-feel, and only partly validated. It is not a comprehension test and not a usability test since nobody interacts. Kuric et al. 2024 argue the 5 s rule of thumb misrepresents cognition: working memory and perceptual speed vary and exposure of 2, 5 and 10 s was tested on pages of varying complexity. Use cloze or highlighter for comprehension of text instead. Summary came from search results only.

title: Seven Rules of Thumb for Web Site Experimenters (Kohavi, Deng, Longbotham, Xu, KDD 2014), landing page
topic: A/B tests: limits for copy tests
rule: Rules are generalised from thousands of controlled experiments at Amazon, Booking.com, LinkedIn and Microsoft and are 'not provably correct'. Page text does not state the rules. Third-party summary (snippet): small changes can have a big effect; big positive wins are rare; your mileage will vary; have enough users. Sample sizes in the paper are in the hundreds of thousands to millions, so a copy A/B test needs traffic that a small site or game lacks.

title: Diagnosing Sample Ratio Mismatch in Online Controlled Experiments (Fabijan, Gupchup, Gupta, Omhover, Qin, Vermeer, Dmitriev, KDD 2019), abstract
rule: If the observed split differs from the planned split, the result is a symptom of a data-quality fault and the experiment cannot be trusted until the cause is found. Ignoring it can make a bad change look good. Based on experiments at four companies across over 25 products. The page gives no prevalence figure or p-value cutoff. A search snippet cites a Kohavi talk where a 50/50 split landing near 50.2% has a one-in-500,000 chance, but I did not read the talk.
example: Check the allocation ratio before reading any copy-test lift.

title: Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi, Tang, Xu 2020), SRM chapter
topic: A/B tests: trust checks (Twyman's law, SRM)
rule: Page returned HTTP 500; only search snippets seen. Book frames SRM as a trust guardrail; Kohavi's 'Twyman's law' advice is that a surprising result should trigger validity checks before shipping. The figure that 8% of experiments are invalid from SRM alone appears in secondary skill sites and was NOT confirmed; do not cite it.

title: Null: no source found tying these tests to LLM-written copy
topic: detecting LLM text with usability tests
rule: Searched NN/g, GDS, 18F, Digital.gov and found nothing measuring cloze, highlighter or A/B tests against model-written versus human-written text. These tests measure whether a reader understands and acts, not who wrote it. The detection panel in judging.md (readers who use LLMs heavily) remains the only measured instrument for 'can you tell'. Also not found: the NN/g five-second and highlighter pages (guessed URLs returned 404), and a sample-size rule for cloze beyond 'as many as possible'.
